blocks.x: All right. Let's see. Now this is an interview being recorded at 818 St. Peter, November the 20-something. What is it? 26th. 28th. It says on your watch, huh? Right. November the 28th, 1959. Because it always says that on my watch. Yes.

People, I think, talk about what is Bill Russell, trying to figure out why he likes it, why he likes this mystery. Because you tend to think, well, there's got to be, Bill has to have some, Bill has a story, there must have been some tragedy or unrequited love or some great plan that ran awry and caused Bill to kind of ignore the rest of humanity. Because it's not fair of me to say this because my, you know, relationship with Bill has been almost non-existent. I don't see Bill that often, but what I, what you just said about Bill kind of ignoring humanity is, I think, at least my experience, has a lot of truth to it. You wonder why, you know, because the constantly, see, the thing is, even though he does this, there are people in and out of that shop all the time. And we both know recluse types down here. Anybody who wants to be a recluse can be a recluse. So, despite the fact that Bill doesn't really try hard to, Bill never really, at least as far as I've ever seen, never really extends himself. He never, politics, never even appears to care whether you come back. But the point is, people do come by and talk to him. And come into the shop and lounge around.

Well, I think Bill was married once, but I've never been able to get the story on that straight. But Alden and David, Alden Ashworth and David Wyckoff, two guys I knew, were down here. And spent a lot of time with Bill. Say that, that he was married, but they don't know any of the details. But I'm sure if he was married, it was to some classical musician, some woman, probably some violin player like him. Was interested in composing a couple of things, probably had a lot in common. Still, it didn't work out on an emotional basis. You can see that.
I wonder about Bill's violin playing. Because Bill is, if there's anything Bill is, about music, he's serious about it.
Mm-hmm.

Recording music and about listening to it and about helping to make music more understandable. The Fellowship, for example. Anything he does relative to band music, he's done in all seriousness. And you would think that with the sensitivity that Bill obviously has, it must be a disappointment to him that he is not a playing musician. You know what I mean? Sure. A collector, I think, must collect partly because it's a compensation form. He either has, I know one of the reasons why I like jazz is because I do not play it and it helps me to participate with it. It's a moving thing. And one of the reasons I collect is because it helps to, oh, it helps associate, it helps you associate with it. It's a kind of compensation for not being able to do it yourself, to become familiar with those people who are doing it.
Well, I feel the same way pretty much about it. I wish that I could play it.
I mean, that's in your own experience.
In my own experience as having studied trombone and found out that I wasn't playing trombone but really studied it.
Yeah.
You know?

Well, it's the same with me. I play at the clarinet in a haphazard fashion. But I'm never going to be any good at it. But you see, you wonder about that because Bill has been so capable. His thermodynamics background, everything he attempts, he seems to do successfully. You wonder about his experience with playing, performing music as a musician.
He might have been more than adequate.

I had to be. But perhaps Bill, being as sensitive as he is, realized that he wasn't going to be, well, I may be overly dramatic about this, but then he realized he wasn't going to be anything more than just competent and that wasn't good enough for him. That wouldn't surprise me. No. There are people, or a lot of people, Bill, that doesn't, and got exclusive right to that. A lot of people who, because of a, you know, a perfectionist war cannot be happy just being competent at a thing. Actually, the world is filled with unhappy people who are unhappy for just that reason. So perhaps, I'm not saying Bill's unhappy. I don't know Bill Warnham to know whether he's happy or unhappy. That might be something interesting to discuss. Do you think he's, do you think Bill is happy?
Myself, I don't. I think Bill's pretty agitated all the time. And he's always running around on a car like that. And he's always worried and anxious and fearful.

So, here's another thing, Dick. This also, I think, has bearing, you know, it's a great American dream when you write a song, you get it published so people will buy it and make you money and you'll become famous. Or when you, well, no matter what form of endeavor you happen to practice, we do it for some sort of reward, material or otherwise. Bill doesn't seem to be seeking any kind of reward, at least any of the rewards that are common. For example, Bill, to my knowledge, is one of the ranking authorities on New Orleans Jazz, maybe the ranking authority. You'd know more about that than I, certainly one of the ranking authorities, probably one of the ranking authorities on jazz, any type, period. Yet Bill has never sought the, well, had never seemed to have received the due that I think he warrants. Now, maybe that's, maybe that's just a cork of fate. Maybe it's, Bill's just unfortunate there. Perhaps Bill, there are a lot of people, of course, of genuine modesty who just do not seek to become famous in the, you know, the great American traditional way. Maybe that has no meaning for Bill. But I'm wondering this, you know, that, I don't know how Bill makes out over there because he sells those records. That's another thing. You go in to buy a record, a 398 record, and by the time Bill gets to discounting it for you because he's had it, these are the standard excuses. He's had it for two years, or he overbought originally and he can't get rid of them, or you're a friend of his, or one of a half a dozen other reasons, or maybe all of them. By the time he gets to discounting it, it's down to where he's making a nickel of record.
Or less.
Or...

I've seen him sell records for less than wholesale many times. And I've seen a woman come in there, a jurist. He never saw that woman before. And he sold her a record for less than wholesale because it was cut out of the catalog and you couldn't get it anymore. Absolutely. And that's a fact.

So it's a wonder to me that Bill can pay the rent over there. And I don't know what other sources of income Bill has, but, you know, a person has to be, I don't care how little money means to a person, you've got to be conscious of money, at least to the extent that you want enough of it at the end of the month to pay the rent and you want to be able to buy food and so on. And I'm sometimes amazed when I think about it, how Bill can provide for the basic necessities. I don't mean that, I'm certainly not, I'm only wondering at why Bill doesn't seem to have a little bit more just healthy interest in just, well, somewhat more share of, than he has had of, of, of note and notoriety for, for his jazz association. And he could be making a little money off it too. He's turned out dozens and dozens of records. Now maybe he's making, maybe that's his chief source of income. I don't know.
But here's a guy. No, he doesn't want to sell records to people. They really don't like them. That's what he thinks. I believe. They don't deserve them. They have no right to them.
Yeah.
Maybe that's it. Which is his privilege. It's his company.

Well, here's a guy who's written, or co-authored some books, who's written a lot of articles, and who has written lots of liner notes, and who is widely quoted in jazz circles, I guess, as most any of the so-called jazz authorities. He's a genuine authority. So, what prompts a guy to write? I guess maybe because he feels the need to say something, and he wants to say it to someone. He can't write in a vacuum. Bill felt that strongly about it. If he had this strong and anti-humanity feeling about him, what I think he ought to do is write and then seal all this stuff in a time capsule to be opened up 100 years after his death, or 10 years after his death. If he doesn't give a damn at all, period, about writing for people, he's got to write for people. And therefore, I'm just wondering, thinking out loud, but I wonder, therefore, because Bill has written, and Bill tries to communicate through his records and his writings and so on, it seems to me to be kind of odd that Bill has had so little share of, well, notoriety. I think he's due a lot more. I think he should have had a lot more.
Well.
Don't you think so?

I think he's gotten enough. I think it's finally coming to him now, you know. As you say, when they quote him, it's just Bill Russell or William Russell, and that is the best kind of a... True. That's the best kind of a thing from a public relations standpoint. He can really... Man, if he can just stand on the basis of just being there.

What do you think Bill wants, Dick? What do you think... If Bill could have anything he wanted, I don't mean any one thing, but if Bill could have a state, any combination of circumstances, what would it be that Bill would want?

Well, first, we better start eliminating it, and just approach it from the negative side. I think the thing that Bill doesn't want really is anything in terms of ordinary material success. He is not interested in that at all, obviously. Here's a guy who doesn't want any more than enough to pay the rent and to eat sandwiches that he's saved for two hours and out of coal. You know, I haven't seen him eat a hot meal since around February, and I don't believe he's had maybe more than one or two hot meals since February. He's just not interested in that kind of thing. He wants enough material things to get by on his standards, which are mighty, mighty low.
No, as a conference, he's not too much interested in.
The conference, no, they don't have to...

And I think, too, if I can interrupt for just one... General... Inject one thought. Bill, I think, objects to invasions of his privacy by the public. If he would become real famous and acknowledge worldwide authority on jazz or recordings or anything less, then the idiot public would invade a lot of the... And this freedom that Bill has now. No, there's no denying. He's got a kind of unique freedom to do as he pleases and do what he wants. Anyway, that's... Go ahead.
Yeah, well, that's right.
He doesn't want that. He doesn't want to become a big authority for... Because it would help... It would probably destroy the thing he has now. But what does he really want?
He wants all the Mardi Gras shoes. And he has a complete collection, obviously. Anything associated with Mardi Gras. Yeah, no, okay. All postcards.

Yeah, and he wants to work on violins. In other words, the things he's doing now, obviously, he enjoys and he pursues them. But let's face it. Here's Bill Russell, a guy... A mystery, really. Not just because Bill defies classification, because a lot of people do that. But Bill is a very capable guy with a great, impressive, and genuine background in music, degrees in music. I think he has degrees in music.
No, physics.
Well, I know. I don't say physics. That's a project. But he has studied... He has studied... He studied on Schoenberg and Powell. Yeah.
And he's had his works performed by major symphonies.

So he's got an undeniably impressive and, that's not the word, genuine background in music, physics, and various other... And these hobbies of his, various other things. I mean, now, is collecting Mardi Gras favors, does it really mean anything to Bill?
Well, it's not...
It doesn't really mean anything. I mean, sure, he wants to get the world's greatest collection, but so what? So he gets the world's greatest collection. Is that going to be...
Well, he's got the world's greatest collection of jazz records, and he never lists his tunes, and started in Missouri. I mean, you know, that's it. You know?

Well, perhaps, perhaps, I'm just questioning at these things, because I don't... I will never understand Bill Russell. Why not? But I really think... I'm going to get another little taste. All right. If I get it right here, I've got ice in my glass.
Okay. Good enough.

But you see, this is being corny about it, but I think that this is a question that applies here. What makes Bill Russell run? Or what makes him tick? And what does he want? I mean, I don't think... All right, this is subjective, and it's my own opinion, and it's based on precious little observation, because I just haven't had that much chance to. And I don't observe Bill as a curiosity. I like Bill as a human being, you know. Sure, we both did. And if I didn't... We both wondered about it. Right. I know hundreds of people that I wouldn't give a damn about not analyzing, but trying to figure out. I could think of a lot better things to do than analyze most anybody I know. But Bill's, as I say, unique. He's not a boy. That's one thing he's not.
You never know.

But, you know, here's a guy with an impressive, genuine background, and most anything that he had, in most many of these little pastimes of his, music, and I mean by that, it's a polishing violin. It's the major occupation of collecting and cataloging records and artists and contributing to the fund of available knowledge about jazz. And even postcards and Mardi Gras favors. All of these things he pursues and is successful at, but dammit is, collecting Mardi Gras favors, you know, it's fine. It's wonderful as a hobby, and Bill has many other hobbies, and this doesn't take up all this time. But I just wonder if this really means anything to Bill. Well, that's why, when I get back to the original question, if Bill could do anything he wanted and have anything he wanted, what do you think it would be? Well, I've got to throw this out,

just for speculation. What about Bill and women getting married and having a family and all that? Right. I think he, I know a girl, she tells me that Bill wanted to marry her at one time, you know. I won't mention her name. I guess you know. This was several years back that this happened. She told me this after she moved her mom. But, I just wondered, is that what Bill wants underneath it all?

Well, Bill is, let's face it, I'm not attempting to dissect Bill or to dismember him. Bill is going to be, would be the most unique of human animals if he could get by without living with a woman for the rest of his life. This is a pretty lonely existence. Oh, sure. So, there's got to be, either Bill has had some unrequited love experience or he hasn't, it's hard to believe that Bill hasn't encountered the right woman yet. He may have not been successful in prevailing upon her.
I think Bill had a baby marriage

or something. Someone under that. Yeah, that might be. But I'm, the only, you see, I don't want to, it's pretentious to say, I feel an anxiety for Bill or I'm sorry for Bill or something like that. Because who am I to feel sorry for Bill Russell? I think Bill, because of his uniqueness is a guy who possesses a lot of the wealth of this, you know, this mortal coil. But at the same time, I do feel sorry for Bill because he, there's a big void someplace and I think probably not having a woman has a lot to do with it. Maybe it. You tend to wonder why a guy is, people, you know, the interesting people you know in life are the unique ones, are the unusual ones. And the usual ones are bores and you avoid them. So, I think this is one of the, helps to explain why Bill has so many people constantly in and out of that shop. People who have a genuine affection for him. But, you wonder, you know, what it is about, in Bill's background that has made him all this unique.

You know, it's a funny thing, I just, this afternoon, picked up a book, I'd never seen it before. You know, there's a copy of it, it's a new book about jazz. And it had one paragraph, and more than one, dealing with Bill, of course, but it had one paragraph that Bill pointed out, you know. There isn't a single thing right in that paragraph, you know. It says, why do people make up things like this? I'm not quoting him perfectly. But it's really true that if you went up to Bill and asked him questions, he would answer them pretty honestly. If you got him in the right mood, like anybody else, you know. And yet, there's so much for Lonely, there's for Lonely written about it, because people are a little too lazy or something to ask him or even write him all out.
This was something somebody had written about it?
Yeah, yeah, it was in a book, paragraph. It was just all Lonely, I remember, because I discussed this subject with Bill.
Oh, I'm not going to ask who wrote it, but this is a new book that has just come out. It's a new book. About New Orleans? About jazz in general. Yeah. Well.
It's just amazing.
Of course, you have to consider, I don't know who this author is, but you've got to consider the author, maybe the guy's an idiot.
No, maybe he is. I don't know, I think he's just imaginative, like so many of the jazz writers.

Well, you know, Bill's colorful. You know, if there's anything, any one little fast summation of Bill Russell, I think you're accurate to say that, he's colorful. So, some fellow writing about New Orleans and the jazz tradition and whatnot might tend to go overboard in describing Bill Russell, who's, you know, apart from the norm.

And that's the funny thing, when Bill writes something, though, it may be colorful, but it's exact, as it can be. He's really describing something that he knows from his experience, or that he's gotten from an eyewitness. He's pretty careful, by the way. About the imputations,

again, unique. Well, Bill is, you know, can't help but admire you and Bill for, I don't know, the, yes, you're welcome. Did I read that as you had written it there? Did I reflect it just right? That's right. It just was all about. I read so much Bill, you know, about, disguised as jazz writing. And you, I know, read a lot more than I have. And you get a little disgusted with these authoritative, pompous, you know, descriptions, and a lot of it's real and accurate. And, also, you begin to, you know, wonder at the motives of some of these people, some of these characters who have, achieved a big name as a jazz authority, but maybe you don't have too much, really, to back it up. And, certainly, Bill Russell, what you and Bill are doing, not only with this fellowship, but, just generally, your enthusiasm for jazz, active enthusiasm, it's one thing to be a fan, but it's another thing to do something about, is good. And I shudder to think what would happen to, you know, this jazz in this city, which, and now, New Orleans traditional, the type of thing that you and Bill are trying to categorize, in another ten years, is, most of these people who are still living now are not going to be around. There's going to be no one to talk to. So, it's a good thing for them, and for jazz, generally, that, that there is someone with as much, uh, integrity as Bill Russell. I shudder to think what, I could think of half a dozen people I'd hate like hell to see handling this thing. Uh, do you know what I mean?
I don't know
what you mean to.
It's a lot of what I think of. But anyway, uh, while we're on the subject of the people who are around here, who have you heard that was really unique and characteristic of New Orleans?
Musicians, you mean?
Yeah. Well,
I don't know names, Dick. I'll tell you what. Well,
band names. It doesn't have to be specific.

Well, the one that comes to my mind soonest, or first, is, uh, Young Tuxedos. Uh, see, not one reason for that is I've heard them more, but, um, I've heard several of the other groups. Uh, of course, being, uh, you know, Yankee and from up north and never having a really, you know, heard any records of these groups. Being able to see them and watch, perhaps watch a parade or a funeral or something, is it, if, if, if, if it's nothing else, it's, uh, unique is a overused word. I've been using it too much, but it's certainly unique, these brands. But the Tuxedos, uh, remember one time it was a parade, this was around Mardi Gras last year, that would be 59, 50 of it this year, February this year, and, uh, I went to a parade over and crossed the river, I think it was in Algiers, I'm not sure, but, oh gee, I think it was a Cornerstone Lang or something. And they had about, don't know the names, but they had about four or five trumpets. I think Kid Thomas was leading the band, if I'm not sure, how come I'm not mistaken. They had a couple of younger fellas who had played, oh, I think one of the guys had played with Ray Charles, for example. Um, some of them had played up in Chicago, some of them had played with some of the better known name bands, I think one had been with Jay McSham. Um, and the, uh, the fire that this, this band breathed, you know, it was really exciting. What the hell is music except it's excitement, it's, it's a, you know, sort of a, uh, organized, uh, regimented excitement. At least that's been my experience. I, for example, I have big enthusiasms for, say, people like Count Basie because it's exciting. I get a kick out of it. It's kicks. And I got as big a kick out of that band, particularly those, those four or five trumpet players that they had who were doing some pretty wild things. One guy, for example, would maybe play the line, whatever they were playing, way up in his third register and another guy would, maybe Kid Thomas would be just kind of blowing it straight. And here, old kid's sort of stumbling along there but you could hear him. Well, and then somebody else would be doing a whole bunch of little figures and arpeggios and the next guy might be playing, say, a counterpoint to that. And Jesus, it was, it was some pretty. So I, that, that, that's a great band. I, in fact, I want to get, they have an album which I want to take with me.

Well, you know, the thing that really gets me about that band, it's a brass band and the other brass bands have air monitors. But it's like Danny Ruffer said about it. If somebody ever recorded that barrel house brass band and it is really barrel house. Now they can sit there and read those directors and play them pretty straight. You know, you've heard that, about it. No deal. Mm-hmm. But God, they can't really get down to the line, you know. See, it's exciting. Yeah.

Well, you know, I think a white person, we've discussed this many times, but we've discussed the merits, as many people have, of white and Negro musicians. Whether there's any point in discussing that or not, it's not the point here. The point is that one thing certain, I think, about any Negro musician is that he certainly knows legitimacy in a jazz band. This is not the discussion of a degree of musicianship or anything of that sort, but if a band has got it, if it breathes as far, and if it swings, if it is Beryl House or however Danny Barker described it, this you don't have to tell. Most any colored person, but you certainly don't have to tell a working colored musician. And they are respectful of a group or an individual or a band that can play this way. And my point is this. Here's this music, this band has had a tradition of members who have been playing under this name for some time now. And it's not just a, because none of the these guys make really any money worth talking about. So it's certainly not that they could go out and pour her, I guess, and make as much money as they're making there. Certainly not exclusively for the money, although that, of course, helps. I don't think this band could have existed and then the other groups, but particularly the Young Tuxedos, because I think it's, of the bands I've heard, the marching, the brass bands I've heard, this is the best. I don't think this band would have existed this long because of the integrity of these people if it hadn't been one damn good band. Now maybe that doesn't, maybe that just doesn't have any meaning at all. Maybe they play if it was, if none of them could play more than, you know, Mickey Mouse.

Well, you know, something that I've really noticed, maybe this is unique to New Orleans, maybe it's just human being, but, it's a band that goes down the street. Just can't help but notice people who come out on their galleries, you know, and it can be anybody. It could be any section of town, any class of people you want to name.
They'll come out and they'll be smiling
and they'll really love to hear that sound, you know.

Well, in the second line, too. The second line depends on where the thing, the parade is or the funeral is, but, if it, say, might be over on this side on the East Bank, you could, you find everybody from high-class uptown, as they call it, down here, to, you know, the real lowlife, walking and strutting in that second line, you wouldn't look twice. You might, it wouldn't be unusual to see, tell you what, when I was first down here, I went to a party, I'd been dying about three weeks, I went to a party out in Metry, which is one of the better sections here in town. Maybe you can tell me the band, I don't even know who it was, but they had a kazoo in the band.
Don't know who that is.
Some guy playing a kazoo. I think it was the old Celestan band, I'm not sure.
They have been.

But, of course, this was a, there were a lot of drunks at this thing, so they tend to be exuberant, but we, there were a couple of old Grand Dane types who were dancing around in a, in a real unusual and un, sort of, un, dignified fashion, who were having a hell of a good time. And you see that. And I don't think you'd see that if this music wasn't pretty legitimate, and wasn't, not just legitimate, if it wasn't pretty exciting music. I don't think jazz is worth a damn unless it's exciting. I don't care how cranial jazz is. I don't care how difficult what is being executed is. If it doesn't excite you, and I don't mean to just, it doesn't have to just do that to excite you, but if there's not something that generates excitement, it is not worth listening to, and it certainly isn't worth playing. That's my point again, because I don't think these people would play it.
Well, they sure don't make anything, you know. People go out and play parades for five dollars up until just recently the scale has been up.
Oh, yeah.
Parades and funerals for five dollars, they're doing it for fun.

I talked to an old guy about a week ago who's not a member of this band, but he's a working musician, his name is Gaino, George Gaino, he plays a banjo. And George was talking, I don't know how much he works, not I guess as much as some musician, but he was really excited about having worked the job and making 16 dollars for, I don't know, five, six hours. Real excited about that. So certainly, and he was excited not because he thought 16 dollars was big money, but it was unusual money, you see. So certainly they're not making this music because everybody figures to get rich doing it. I don't guess music down here would have lasted as long, this unique New Orleans music, if the musicians were only interested in getting rich because they'd all be up in Chicago or they'd all be someplace else. Musicians starved down here, by any standard. But there's something, I don't know how much more space we've got here, but I'd say a band I like that a lot of people kind of put down because maybe they hear it a lot is the Paddock Lounge band that's up on Bourbon Street, the Bill Matthews band. There aren't any real outstanding soloists in the band, Wallace Davenport used to be with them, but I never heard him do anything real tasty and he was sort of playing a little bit out of his idiom, at least he didn't sign to them too. But the band was a pretty good, I think for some tourists from Moline, Illinois walking off the street would walk in and would be fortunate to hear it because it's a pretty good representation of New Orleans music. And then there are a lot of white musicians too down here who play pretty good music. I mean I would mention, I think probably because I know him, but I would also mention him because I believe what he does is I get a kick out of Paul Crocker. I like Paul. I like Paul Crocker.
Memorial Award. Okay. Yeah. Well, I mentioned Paul Crawford. I was, I can...
